scope_notes: OAuth v2 bot token grant. v1 is retired.
chat:write posts messages, channels:read lists public channels, channels:history reads them.
channels:join lets the bot join a public channel it was never invited to. Without it every unjoined channel answers not_in_channel and syncs nothing.
users:read resolves the user ids that conversations.history returns.

sync.prompt: Choose which Slack channels to sync

dimensions.label: Channels
dimensions.note: No new node: slack-list_channels-1 already lists exactly what a person picks from, and option_mapping turns its channels into scope options. The name goes in without a leading #, because the four value-expression operators cannot join two strings; `kind: channel` is what draws the # in the picker. num_members is a number and an option's sublabel is text, so the member count waits for either a formatting operator or a sublabel the runtime renders.

channel_day.label: Channel days
channel_day.note: One document per channel per day, holding the messages that are not part of a thread plus a one-line stub for every thread that started that day. message_count is the engine's own record_count, participants is the engine's own participants, and threads is an array so a reader counts them with its length. first_time and thread_count are NOT stored: the bucket merge keeps the last value per key, which is right for last_time and wrong for a first or a sum, and the day's first clock time is already the document's first line. posted_time is the record's own time: merged into the day it is the newest line's time, and read off a single record it is when a file carried by that line was posted.

thread.label: Threads
thread.note: A thread is its own document, root and every reply, however many days it spans. That is what stops a thread growing tomorrow from rewriting yesterday's channel day. The node emits every line with its own document_key, so the two Slack objects read ONE list node and each takes its own records through `when`; is_thread_record is a field because the four operators cannot say 'not'. Every thread fact (reply_count, started_by, last_reply_time, file_count) is stamped identically on every line, because the bucket merge keeps the LAST value per key and only a constant survives that honestly. `in_container` rather than a new 'started_in' kind: the four link kinds the schema allows already name this edge, and a fifth needs a migration. The page is 100 messages, not 200, because the node reads the replies of every thread root on the page and the page size is the only bound on that.

rate_limit_notes: Slack limits per METHOD, in tiers, not per app.
Tier 1 ~1/min, Tier 2 ~20/min (conversations.list), Tier 3 ~50/min (conversations.history, conversations.replies, conversations.info, users.list).
chat.postMessage is the special tier: about 1 message per second PER CHANNEL.

rate_limits is one bucket per app, and it is set to Tier 3 — 50 a minute — because every call a SYNC makes is Tier 3. At 20 a minute one busy channel page cost five minutes and a background crawl was killed before it finished.

The one Tier 2 method these nodes touch is conversations.list, which the picker calls a handful of times when a person opens it, never in a loop. Slack answers 429 with Retry-After and the framework pauses this connection's bucket for exactly that long, so overshooting a slower tier costs latency and never costs correctness.
burst lets a small batch through, which is the shape almost every call has.
The per-channel second is NOT enforced here — one app-wide bucket cannot express a per-channel rule. slack-send_messages-1 owns it by sending one channel's messages in order.
One bucket for every method. Per-node limits are the upgrade path the day a node needs Tier 4 throughput.
